sdVisual.title: Start here
sdVisual.text: At 2.5 years, interviewers check two things: can you design a small system cleanly (LLD), and can you talk sensibly about a big one (HLD). Expectations vary by company, but LLD is often the bigger filter and HLD is expected at a basic level. Where to begin Rounds you may see Service companies lean on OOP, Java and project questions. Product companies and startups usually add a machine coding (LLD) round and a lighter HLD round. How to split your time LLD / machine coding (60 min) HLD discussion (45 min) What is expected at 2.5 years LLD Clean classes with clear jobs, SOLID in plain words, 4 to 5 patterns used naturally, working code in 60 to 90 minutes, and basic thread-safety. HLD A clear framework, the standard building blocks (load balancer, cache, database, queue), rough numbers, and honest trade-offs. You are not expected to design a Google-scale system alone. Four-week plan Good questions to ask the interviewer Who are the users and how many? What matters more here: speed, correctness or cost? Can I assume a single country and currency? Is it okay to skip login and payments for now? Should I focus on code or on the diagram?

Use a pattern only when you can name the change it protects against. God class One ParkingManager doing everything. Give each class one job. Ignoring concurrency Two users booking the same seat or spot. Mention locking even if you do not fully code it.

sdVisual.title: LRU Cache (HashMap + linked list)
sdVisual.text: Keep a HashMap for O(1) lookup and a doubly linked list for order. Newest item sits at the front. When full, drop the item at the back. Try it key value put(key, value) get(key) Reset Linked list: most recent first (capacity 3) Step log Understand the design Requirements Functional get(key) returns the value or -1 put(key, value) inserts or updates When full, remove the least recently used key Non-functional get and put in O(1) Thread-safe if shared across requests Capacity fixed at creation Core objects (nouns become classes) LRUCache : the public API: get, put, capacity Node : one entry: key, value, prev, next HashMap<K, Node> : jump straight to a node in O(1) Doubly linked list : keeps order: most recent at head, least recent at tail Class diagram head, tail map points to LRUCache -capacity: int -map: Map<K, Node> -head, tail: Node +get(key): V +put(key, value) -moveToFront(node) -removeTail() Node key: K value: V prev, next: Node java.util HashMap key -> Node get / put / remove: O(1) extends implements owns (composition) has (aggregation) uses Design decisions and patterns Decision Pattern / idea Why Why a HashMap? Index Finding a key in a list is O(n). The map gives the node directly. Why a doubly linked list? Order tracking Removing a node from the middle needs prev and next pointers, so it is O(1). Dummy head and tail nodes Sentinel nodes No null checks when the list is empty or has one item. Store key inside Node Back-reference When we evict the tail we must also remove its key from the map. Concurrency: what can go wrong with many threads Two threads calling put at the same time can corrupt prev/next pointers. Simple fix: mark get and put synchronized . Faster: ReentrantReadWriteLock does not help much because get also moves nodes, so it is a write. In real projects use Caffeine or LinkedHashMap wrapped with Collections.synchronizedMap . Walk the code Complete but small. Read it top to bottom: each class does one job. LRUCache.java (HashMap + doubly linked list) class LRUCache { private class Node { int key, value; Node prev, next; Node(int k, int v) { key = k; value = v; } } private final int capacity; private final Map<Integer, Node> map = new HashMap<>(); private final Node head = new Node(0, 0); // dummy: most recent after this private final Node tail = new Node(0, 0); // dummy: least recent before this LRUCache(int capacity) { this.capacity = capacity; head.next = tail; tail.prev = head; } public synchronized int get(int key) { Node n = map.get(key); if (n == null) return -1; remove(n); // take it out of its place addFirst(n); // put it at the front: just used return n.value; } public synchronized void put(int key, int value) { Node n = map.get(key); if (n != null) { // update existing n.value = value; remove(n); addFirst(n); return; } if (map.size() == capacity) { // full: evict least recent Node lru = tail.prev; remove(lru); map.remove(lru.key); } Node fresh = new Node(key, value); addFirst(fresh); map.put(key, fresh); } private void remove(Node n) { n.prev.next = n.next; n.next.prev = n.prev; } private void addFirst(Node n) { n.next = head.next; n.prev = head; head.next.prev = n; head.next = n; } } Shortcut: LinkedHashMap (say it, then build the real one) class LRUCache<K, V> extends LinkedHashMap<K, V> { private final int capacity; LRUCache(int capacity) { super(capacity, 0.75f, true); // true = access order this.capacity = capacity; } @Override protected boolean removeEldestEntry(Map.Entry<K, V> eldest) { return size() > capacity; // evict when over capacity } } Follow-up questions interviewers ask How would you add expiry (TTL)? Store an expiresAt in each Node. On get, if expired, remove it and return -1. Optionally a background thread cleans up expired nodes. How is LFU different? LFU evicts the key used the fewest times. Keep a map from frequency to a linked list of nodes and track the minimum frequency. Still O(1). How would you make it distributed? Use Redis with maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru, or shard k

sdVisual.title: Tic-Tac-Toe design (Board, Player, Game)
sdVisual.text: Three small classes: Board stores cells, Player has a symbol, Game runs turns and checks the winner. Play below, then read the diagram. Try it New game Click a cell Step log Class diagram Game Board board Player[] players int turn play(row, col) Board char[3][3] cells place(r, c, symbol) hasWinner(symbol) Player String name char symbol has 1 has 2 Understand the design Requirements Functional Two players take turns on a 3x3 board Detect a win (row, column, diagonal) or a draw Reject moves on taken cells Non-functional Easy to extend to N x N and more players Win check in O(1) per move Clear separation: rules vs display Core objects (nouns become classes) Game : controls turns and the game status Board : holds the cells and checks wins Player : name and symbol (X or O) Move : row and column chosen by a player GameStatus : IN_PROGRESS, WIN, DRAW Class diagram owns 2 players Game -board: Board -players: Player[] -turn: int -status: GameStatus +play(row, col): GameStatus -switchTurn() Board -n: int -cells: char[][] -rows, cols: int[] -diag, anti: int +place(r, c, p): boolean +isFull(): boolean Player -name: String -symbol: char <<enum>> GameStatus IN_PROGRESS WIN, DRAW extends implements owns (composition) has (aggregation) uses Design decisions and patterns Decision Pattern / idea Why Board knows the rules of a win Single Responsibility Game handles turns; Board handles cells and win checks. Counter arrays for rows/cols/diagonals O(1) win check Add +1 for X and -1 for O. A row is won when its counter hits +n or -n. No scanning. Player as its own class Open/Closed Later a ComputerPlayer can extend Player and choose moves itself. Enum for status Type safety No magic strings like "win". Concurrency: what can go wrong with many threads Usually single-threaded. For an online version, each game is handled by one thread or guarded by a lock per game so two moves cannot be applied at once. Walk the code Complete but small. Read it top to bottom: each class does one job. Board, Player, Game enum GameStatus { IN_PROGRESS, WIN, DRAW } record Player(String name, char symbol) {} class Board { private final int n; private final char[][] cells; private final int[] rows, cols; private int diag, anti, filled; Board(int n) { this.n = n; cells = new char[n][n]; rows = new int[n]; cols = new int[n]; } /** returns true if this move wins */ boolean place(int r, int c, char symbol) { if (r < 0 || c < 0 || r >= n || c >= n || cells[r][c] != 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Invalid move"); cells[r][c] = symbol; filled++; int add = symbol == 'X' ? 1 : -1; rows[r] += add; cols[c] += add; if (r == c) diag += add; if (r + c == n - 1) anti += add; return Math.abs(rows[r]) == n || Math.abs(cols[c]) == n || Math.abs(diag) == n || Math.abs(anti) == n; } boolean isFull() { return filled == n * n; } } class Game { private final Board board = new Board(3); private final Player[] players; private int turn = 0; private GameStatus status = GameStatus.IN_PROGRESS; Game(Player a, Player b) { players = new Player[]{a, b}; } GameStatus play(int r, int c) { if (status != GameStatus.IN_PROGRESS) throw new IllegalStateException("Game over"); Player p = players[turn]; if (board.place(r, c, p.symbol())) status = GameStatus.WIN; else if (board.isFull()) status = GameStatus.DRAW; else turn = 1 - turn; // next player return status; } } Follow-up questions interviewers ask How do you support N x N? Board already takes n. The counter arrays scale with n and the check stays O(1). How do you add a computer player? Make Player an interface with nextMove(Board). HumanPlayer reads input; ComputerPlayer picks a move (random or minimax). Strategy pattern. Undo a move? Keep a stack of moves. Undo pops the last move and reverses the counter changes. How would you save and resume? Store the move list. Replaying the moves rebuilds the board. Common mistakes Scanning the whole board after each move It works, but the counter trick is the answer interviewers hope for. Game class doing ever

sdVisual.text: The machine behaves differently in each state . Draw the states, then list what each button does in each state. Item price is 20. Try it Insert coin (10) Select item Cancel Reset States and transitions Step log Understand the design Requirements Functional Insert coins and keep credit Select an item; dispense if credit is enough Return change; cancel refunds credit Track stock per item Non-functional Easy to add new states (OutOfService, Maintenance) Never dispense without enough money One customer at a time Core objects (nouns become classes) VendingMachine : holds credit, inventory and the current state State : interface: insertCoin, select, cancel IdleState, HasMoneyState, DispensingState : one class per state Inventory : item code to price and count Coin : enum of accepted values Class diagram current VendingMachine -state: State -credit: int -inventory: Inventory +insertCoin(c) +select(code) +cancel() ~setState(s) <<interface>> State insertCoin(m, c) select(m, code) cancel(m) IdleState ... HasMoneyState ... DispensingState ... Inventory -items: Map<String, Item> +price(code) +take(code) extends implements owns (composition) has (aggregation) uses Design decisions and patterns Decision Pattern / idea Why One class per state State pattern Each class answers "what does this button do in this state?" No giant switch. Machine delegates to state Delegation machine.select() just calls state.select(this). Behaviour changes when the state object changes. States are stateless singletons Flyweight IdleState has no fields, so one shared instance is enough. Inventory separate Single Responsibility Stock and prices change for different reasons than state logic. Concurrency: what can go wrong with many threads If the machine is controlled by a server (many requests), wrap the public methods in synchronized so two selects cannot both dispense the last item. Walk the code Complete but small. Read it top to bottom: each class does one job. State pattern: the full machine interface State { void insertCoin(VendingMachine m, int amount); void select(VendingMachine m, String code); void cancel(VendingMachine m); } class IdleState implements State { public void insertCoin(VendingMachine m, int amount) { m.addCredit(amount); m.setState(new HasMoneyState()); } public void select(VendingMachine m, String code) { System.out.println("Insert coin first"); } public void cancel(VendingMachine m) { System.out.println("Nothing to cancel"); } } class HasMoneyState implements State { public void insertCoin(VendingMachine m, int amount) { m.addCredit(amount); } public void select(VendingMachine m, String code) { int price = m.inventory().price(code); if (!m.inventory().inStock(code)) { System.out.println("Sold out"); return; } if (m.credit() < price) { System.out.println("Need " + (price - m.credit()) + " more"); return; } m.setState(new DispensingState()); m.inventory().take(code); m.refund(m.credit() - price); // change m.setState(new IdleState()); } public void cancel(VendingMachine m) { m.refund(m.credit()); m.setState(new IdleState()); } } class DispensingState implements State { public void insertCoin(VendingMachine m, int a) { System.out.println("Please wait"); } public void select(VendingMachine m, String c) { System.out.println("Please wait"); } public void cancel(VendingMachine m) { System.out.println("Too late to cancel"); } } class VendingMachine { private State state = new IdleState(); private int credit; private final Inventory inventory = new Inventory(); public synchronized void insertCoin(int a) { state.insertCoin(this, a); } public synchronized void select(String c) { state.select(this, c); } public synchronized void cancel() { state.cancel(this); } void setState(State s) { state = s; } void addCredit(int a) { credit += a; } int credit() { return credit; } void refund(int a) { System.out.println("Refund " + a); credit = 0; } Inventory inventory() { return inventory; } } Follow-up questions interviewers ask Add an OutOfService state? sdVisual.text: Vehicles need a slot of the right size. Find the first free slot that fits, give a ticket, and charge by hours on exit. Click a filled slot to unpark. Try it Park Bike Park Car Park Truck hours Reset Slots: S = small, M = medium, L = large (rate per hour 10 / 20 / 40) Step log Understand the design Requirements Functional Park bikes, cars and trucks in slots that fit Issue a ticket on entry Charge on exit by hours and slot type Show free slots per floor Non-functional Many entry gates at once: no two vehicles get one slot Pricing rules change often Add floors and vehicle types easily Core objects (nouns become classes) ParkingLot : entry point: park and unpark Floor : a list of slots Slot : id, size, occupied flag Vehicle : abstract; Bike, Car, Truck Ticket : vehicle, slot, entry time PricingStrategy : computes the fee Class diagram 1..* 1..* uses ParkingLot -floors: List<Floor> -pricing: PricingStrategy +park(v): Ticket +unpark(t): long Floor -slots: List<Slot> +findSlot(size): Slot Slot -id: String -size: Size -taken: AtomicBoolean +tryOccupy(): boolean +free() Ticket -vehicle: Vehicle -slot: Slot -entry: Instant <<abstract>> Vehicle -plate: String +size(): Size <<interface>> PricingStrategy +fee(ticket, exit): long Car Bike Truck HourlyPricing +fee(...) extends implements owns (composition) has (aggregation) uses Design decisions and patterns Decision Pattern / idea Why Pricing as an interface Strategy pattern Weekend rates, flat rates or EV charging plug in as new classes. Vehicle hierarchy with size() Polymorphism Slot matching asks vehicle.size(), never "if car else if bike". Slot.tryOccupy() with AtomicBoolean Compare-and-set Two gates cannot take the same slot. ParkingLot as the only public API Facade Gates call park/unpark; floors and slots stay hidden. Concurrency: what can go wrong with many threads Two entry gates may find the same free slot at the same time. If both set taken = true , one car is lost. Use taken.compareAndSet(false, true) : only one gate succeeds, the other moves on to the next slot. Walk the code Complete but small. Read it top to bottom: each class does one job. Parking lot core classes enum Size { SMALL, MEDIUM, LARGE } abstract class Vehicle { final String plate; Vehicle(String plate) { this.plate = plate; } abstract Size size(); } class Bike extends Vehicle { Bike(String p) { super(p); } Size size() { return Size.SMALL; } } class Car extends Vehicle { Car(String p) { super(p); } Size size() { return Size.MEDIUM; } } class Truck extends Vehicle { Truck(String p) { super(p); } Size size() { return Size.LARGE; } } class Slot { final String id; final Size size; private final AtomicBoolean taken = new AtomicBoolean(false); Slot(String id, Size size) { this.id = id; this.size = size; } boolean fits(Vehicle v) { return size.ordinal() >= v.size().ordinal(); } boolean tryOccupy() { return taken.compareAndSet(false, true); } // atomic void free() { taken.set(false); } } record Ticket(Vehicle vehicle, Slot slot, Instant entry) {} interface PricingStrategy { long fee(Ticket t, Instant exit); } class HourlyPricing implements PricingStrategy { private final Map<Size, Long> rate = Map.of(Size.SMALL, 10L, Size.MEDIUM, 20L, Size.LARGE, 40L); public long fee(Ticket t, Instant exit) { long hours = Math.max(1, (Duration.between(t.entry(), exit).toMinutes() + 59) / 60); return hours * rate.get(t.slot().size); } } class ParkingLot { private final List<Slot> slots; private final PricingStrategy pricing; ParkingLot(List<Slot> slots, PricingStrategy pricing) { this.slots = slots; this.pricing = pricing; } Ticket park(Vehicle v) { for (Slot s : slots) if (s.fits(v) && s.tryOccupy()) // first fitting free slot return new Ticket(v, s, Instant.now()); throw new IllegalStateException("Lot full"); } long unpark(Ticket t) { t.slot().free(); return pricing.fee(t, Instant.now()); } } Follow-up questions interviewers ask How to find a slot faster than a linear scan? sdVisual.title: Elevator (SCAN algorithm)
sdVisual.text: Keep moving in one direction and serve every request on the way. When none remain ahead, turn around. This is the SCAN idea (like a disk arm). Try it floors 0 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 Run elevator Reset Shaft (floor 7 on top). Amber = requested Step log Understand the design Requirements Functional Request an elevator from a floor (up or down) Choose a floor from inside the car Move and stop at requested floors Doors open and close Non-functional Short waiting time No starvation: every request served Easy to change the scheduling rule Safe: never move with doors open Core objects (nouns become classes) ElevatorSystem : takes requests and assigns cars Elevator : current floor, direction, stops Request : floor and direction Direction : UP, DOWN, IDLE Scheduler : strategy that picks the car and next stop Class diagram 1..* uses ElevatorSystem -cars: List<Elevator> -scheduler: Scheduler +request(floor, dir) <<interface>> Scheduler +pick(cars, req): Elevator NearestCarScheduler +pick(...) Elevator -floor: int -dir: Direction -up: TreeSet<Integer> -down: TreeSet<Integer> +addStop(f) +step() <<enum>> Direction UP, DOWN, IDLE Request -floor: int -dir: Direction extends implements owns (composition) has (aggregation) uses Design decisions and patterns Decision Pattern / idea Why SCAN (keep going one way) Elevator algorithm Serve every stop in the current direction, then turn. No request waits forever. Two sorted sets of stops TreeSet up.ceiling(floor) gives the next stop above; down.floor(floor) the next below. Scheduler as a strategy Strategy pattern Switch from "nearest car" to "least busy car" without touching Elevator. Elevator state machine State idea Moving, DoorsOpen, Idle make illegal actions impossible. Concurrency: what can go wrong with many threads Requests arrive from many floors on different threads while the car moves. Guard the stop sets with synchronized (or use ConcurrentSkipListSet ), and run each car's movement loop on its own thread. Walk the code Complete but small. Read it top to bottom: each class does one job. Elevator with SCAN enum Direction { UP, DOWN, IDLE } class Elevator { private int floor = 0; private Direction dir = Direction.IDLE; private final TreeSet<Integer> up = new TreeSet<>(); private final TreeSet<Integer> down = new TreeSet<>(); synchronized void addStop(int f) { if (f > floor) up.add(f); else if (f < floor) down.add(f); if (dir == Direction.IDLE) dir = f > floor ? Direction.UP : Direction.DOWN; } /** move one step; called by a timer or loop */ synchronized void step() { if (dir == Direction.UP) { Integer next = up.ceiling(floor); if (next == null) { dir = down.isEmpty() ? Direction.IDLE : Direction.DOWN; return; } floor++; if (floor == next) { up.remove(next); openDoors(); } } else if (dir == Direction.DOWN) { Integer next = down.floor(floor); if (next == null) { dir = up.isEmpty() ? Direction.IDLE : Direction.UP; return; } floor--; if (floor == next) { down.remove(next); openDoors(); } } } int floor() { return floor; } Direction dir() { return dir; } private void openDoors() { System.out.println("Doors open at " + floor); } } interface Scheduler { Elevator pick(List<Elevator> cars, int floor); } class NearestCarScheduler implements Scheduler { public Elevator pick(List<Elevator> cars, int floor) { return cars.stream() .min(Comparator.comparingInt(e -> Math.abs(e.floor() - floor))) .orElseThrow(); } } class ElevatorSystem { private final List<Elevator> cars; private final Scheduler scheduler; ElevatorSystem(List<Elevator> cars, Scheduler s) { this.cars = cars; this.scheduler = s; } void request(int floor) { scheduler.pick(cars, floor).addStop(floor); } } Follow-up questions interviewers ask Why not first-come-first-served? The car would zig-zag (floor 9, then 1, then 8). SCAN serves everything on the way, which is faster overall. Better car choice? sdVisual.title: Splitwise (simplify debts)
sdVisual.text: Add expenses split equally. Track each person's net balance (paid minus share). Then match biggest debtor with biggest creditor to cut the number of payments. Try it payer Asha Ravi Meena Kiran amount Add expense (split 4 ways) Sample trip Reset Balances and simplified payments Step log Understand the design Requirements Functional Add an expense paid by one person and split among many Split equally, by exact amounts or by percent Show who owes whom Simplify debts to fewer payments Non-functional Money must add up exactly (no rounding loss) Groups of up to a few hundred people History of every expense Core objects (nouns become classes) User : id and name Group : members and expenses Expense : payer, amount, splits Split : user and share; EqualSplit, ExactSplit, PercentSplit BalanceSheet : net balance per user DebtSimplifier : turns balances into minimal payments Class diagram 1..* 1..* uses paid by Group -members: List<User> -expenses: List<Expense> +addExpense(e) +balances(): Map Expense -paidBy: User -amount: long -splits: List<Split> <<abstract>> Split -user: User -share: long EqualSplit ExactSplit PercentSplit -percent DebtSimplifier +simplify(balances): List<Payment> User -id -name extends implements owns (composition) has (aggregation) uses Design decisions and patterns Decision Pattern / idea Why Store money as long paise Exactness Doubles lose fractions (0.1 + 0.2 is not 0.3). Split types as subclasses Polymorphism / Strategy Each split type validates itself (exact amounts must add up, percents to 100). Net balance per user Simplification Only the final +/- per person matters, not who paid whom. Greedy max creditor and max debtor Two heaps Repeatedly settle the biggest debtor with the biggest creditor: at most n - 1 payments. Concurrency: what can go wrong with many threads Two people adding expenses to the same group at once can lose an update to the balance map. Recompute balances from the expense list, or update balances inside a lock / DB transaction per group. Walk the code Complete but small. Read it top to bottom: each class does one job. Balances and debt simplification record Payment(String from, String to, long amount) {} class Group { private final Map<String, Long> balance = new HashMap<>(); // + means is owed, - means owes /** equal split: payer paid amount for everyone in 'members' */ synchronized void addEqualExpense(String payer, long amountPaise, List<String> members) { long share = amountPaise / members.size(); long leftover = amountPaise - share * members.size(); // e.g. 100 / 3 leaves 1 for (String m : members) balance.merge(m, -share, Long::sum); balance.merge(payer, amountPaise - leftover, Long::sum); // payer absorbs the leftover paise } List<Payment> simplify() { PriorityQueue<Map.Entry<String, Long>> creditors = new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> Long.compare(b.getValue(), a.getValue())); PriorityQueue<Map.Entry<String, Long>> debtors = new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> Long.compare(a.getValue(), b.getValue())); for (var e : balance.entrySet()) { if (e.getValue() > 0) creditors.add(new AbstractMap.SimpleEntry<>(e)); if (e.getValue() < 0) debtors.add(new AbstractMap.SimpleEntry<>(e)); } List<Payment> out = new ArrayList<>(); while (!creditors.isEmpty() && !debtors.isEmpty()) { var c = creditors.poll(); var d = debtors.poll(); long pay = Math.min(c.getValue(), -d.getValue()); out.add(new Payment(d.getKey(), c.getKey(), pay)); if (c.getValue() - pay > 0) { c.setValue(c.getValue() - pay); creditors.add(c); } if (d.getValue() + pay < 0) { d.setValue(d.getValue() + pay); debtors.add(d); } } return out; // at most n - 1 payments } } Follow-up questions interviewers ask Is greedy always the minimum number of payments? Not always (the true minimum is NP-hard), but greedy gives at most n - 1 payments and is what real apps use. How do you handle percent splits? PercentSplit validates the percents add to 100, computes each share, and gives the rounding remainder to one person. Multiple currencies? Store currency p

sdVisual.text: Two users click the same seat at nearly the same time. Without a lock both can book it. Use an atomic hold (lock or compare-and-set) so only one wins. Try it No lock (bug) Atomic hold (fix) Both click seat A1 Reset Timeline of two requests Step log Understand the design Requirements Functional Show seat map for a show Hold seats for a user for 10 minutes Confirm on payment, release on timeout or cancel Non-functional Never sell one seat twice Holds expire automatically Fast under flash-sale load Core objects (nouns become classes) Show : movie, screen, start time Seat : row, number, status SeatHold : user, seats, expiresAt Booking : confirmed seats and payment SeatLockProvider : interface: lock and unlock seats BookingService : orchestrates hold, pay, confirm Class diagram uses creates creates BookingService -locks: SeatLockProvider -repo: BookingRepository +hold(show, seats, user): SeatHold +confirm(holdId, payment): Booking <<interface>> SeatLockProvider +lock(show, seats, user, ttl): boolean +unlock(show, seats, user) InMemoryLockProvider -map: ConcurrentHashMap RedisLockProvider SET NX EX SeatHold -user -seats: List<Seat> -expiresAt: Instant Booking -id -seats -paymentId -status extends implements owns (composition) has (aggregation) uses Design decisions and patterns Decision Pattern / idea Why Lock provider as interface Dependency Inversion In-memory for the interview, Redis in production. Same service code. Hold with expiry, not a DB lock Optimistic temporary hold Users can take minutes to pay; DB locks would block everyone. putIfAbsent / SET NX Atomic check-and-set The check "is it free?" and the write "now it is mine" must be one step. Unique constraint on (show, seat) Last line of defence Even if the lock layer fails, the DB refuses a second booking. Concurrency: what can go wrong with many threads The bug: two threads both read "seat is free", then both write "booked". Fix with an atomic operation: ConcurrentHashMap.putIfAbsent in memory, SET key value NX EX 600 in Redis, or SELECT ... FOR UPDATE / a unique index in SQL. Lock multiple seats in a fixed order (sorted ids) to avoid deadlock, and roll back all if one fails. Walk the code Complete but small. Read it top to bottom: each class does one job. Atomic seat hold (in memory) record HoldKey(String showId, String seatId) {} record Hold(String userId, Instant expiresAt) { boolean expired() { return Instant.now().isAfter(expiresAt); } } class InMemorySeatLocks { private final ConcurrentHashMap<HoldKey, Hold> holds = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); /** all-or-nothing hold of several seats */ boolean lock(String show, List<String> seats, String user, Duration ttl) { List<String> sorted = seats.stream().sorted().toList(); // fixed order List<HoldKey> taken = new ArrayList<>(); Hold mine = new Hold(user, Instant.now().plus(ttl)); for (String seat : sorted) { HoldKey k = new HoldKey(show, seat); holds.computeIfPresent(k, (key, h) -> h.expired() ? null : h); // drop expired hold if (holds.putIfAbsent(k, mine) != null) { // atomic taken.forEach(holds::remove); // roll back return false; } taken.add(k); } return true; } void unlock(String show, List<String> seats, String user) { for (String s : seats) holds.computeIfPresent(new HoldKey(show, s), (k, h) -> h.userId().equals(user) ? null : h); } } class BookingService { private final InMemorySeatLocks locks = new InMemorySeatLocks(); boolean hold(String show, List<String> seats, String user) { return locks.lock(show, seats, user, Duration.ofMinutes(10)); } void confirm(String show, List<String> seats, String user, String paymentId) { // INSERT INTO booking_seats(show_id, seat_id, ...) -- UNIQUE(show_id, seat_id) locks.unlock(show, seats, user); } } Follow-up questions interviewers ask How does it work across many servers? In-memory locks only work on one JVM. Use Redis SET NX EX (or Redisson), plus the DB unique constraint. What if payment succeeds after the hold expired? sdVisual.title: Concurrency basics: race, deadlock, buffer
sdVisual.text: Three bugs interviewers love: race condition (lost update), deadlock (two threads wait on each other), and the producer-consumer buffer. Try it Three mini labs Step log Lab A: lost update (two threads, count++) Run without sync Run with synchronized Lab B: deadlock Threads take locks in opposite order Same order (fixed) Lab C: producer-consumer (buffer size 4) Produce Consume Run 12 random steps Reset Understand the design Requirements Functional Understand race conditions and how to prevent them Spot and fix deadlocks Coordinate producer and consumer threads Non-functional Correct first, then fast Prefer high-level tools (java.util.concurrent) over raw wait/notify Core objects (nouns become classes) Thread : a path of execution Shared state : data more than one thread touches Lock / synchronized : lets one thread at a time into a critical section Atomic classes : lock-free single-variable updates (AtomicInteger) BlockingQueue : thread-safe queue that waits when full or empty ExecutorService : a pool of reusable threads Class diagram put take runs runs Producer -queue: BlockingQueue +run(): put(x) <<interface>> BlockingQueue capacity: 4 put(x): waits if full take(): waits if empty Consumer -queue: BlockingQueue +run(): take() <<interface>> ExecutorService submit(task) shutdown() Counter -count: AtomicInteger +inc() extends implements owns (composition) has (aggregation) uses Design decisions and patterns Decision Pattern / idea Why count++ is three steps Read, add, write Two threads can read the same old value, so one update is lost. synchronized or AtomicInteger Mutual exclusion / CAS Either makes the update one indivisible step. Always take locks in the same order Lock ordering Deadlock needs a cycle (A waits for B, B waits for A). A global order makes a cycle impossible. BlockingQueue for producer-consumer Hand-off put waits when full, take waits when empty. No manual wait/notify. Thread pool, not new Thread() ExecutorService Creating threads is expensive; pools reuse them and limit how many run. Concurrency: what can go wrong with many threads Four conditions must all hold for a deadlock: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, circular wait. Break any one. The easiest in code is circular wait: order your locks. Also use tryLock(timeout) from ReentrantLock to back off instead of waiting forever. Walk the code Complete but small. Read it top to bottom: each class does one job. Race fix, deadlock fix, producer-consumer // 1) Race condition fix class Counter { private final AtomicInteger count = new AtomicInteger(); void inc() { count.incrementAndGet(); } // atomic, no lost updates int get() { return count.get(); } } // 2) Deadlock fix: always lock the lower id first void transfer(Account a, Account b, long amt) { Account first = a.id < b.id ? a : b; Account second = a.id < b.id ? b : a; synchronized (first) { synchronized (second) { a.balance -= amt; b.balance += amt; } } } // 3) Producer-consumer with a bounded buffer BlockingQueue<Integer> q = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(4); ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2); pool.submit(() -> { // producer for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) q.put(i); // waits when 4 items are inside return null; }); pool.submit(() -> { // consumer for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) System.out.println(q.take()); // waits when empty return null; }); pool.shutdown(); Follow-up questions interviewers ask synchronized vs ReentrantLock? Both give mutual exclusion. ReentrantLock adds tryLock with timeout, fairness, and multiple conditions. Use synchronized for simple cases. What does volatile do? Makes writes visible to other threads immediately, but does not make count++ atomic. ConcurrentHashMap vs synchronizedMap? ConcurrentHashMap locks small parts (buckets), so many threads read and write at once. synchronizedMap locks the whole map. How do you find a deadlock in production? Take a thread dump (jstack). It shows threads BLOCKED waiting on each other's locks. Common mistakes Thinking volatile f

Say the extras (locks, patterns, DB) in words. Common mistakes Starting to code before listing requirements, one giant class, forgetting to run the sample scenario at the end. sdVisual.title: The HLD interview: a 4-step game plan
sdVisual.text: A system design round is not a quiz with one right answer. It is a conversation where you show you can take a vague idea, ask the right questions, sketch a working system, then make it survive real traffic. Follow the same 4 steps every time and you will never freeze. The 45 minutes, at a glance 1. Needs 2. Numbers 3. High-level design (15 min) 4. Deep dive (15 min) 5. Wrap-up Requirements 5 min, numbers 5 min, design 15 min, deep dive 15 min, wrap-up 5 min. Click a block or use the buttons below. The running example is "Design Instagram" (post photos, follow people, see a feed). Walk through it on a real example ← Previous step Next step → What the interviewer is scoring Signal What good looks like Red flag Problem scoping Asks about users, scale, must-have features. Writes them down. Starts drawing boxes in minute one. High-level design A simple, complete diagram where every requirement maps to a box. Missing pieces (where are photos stored?) or 20 boxes with no reason. Depth Goes deep on the hardest part (feed, consistency, hot users). Stays shallow everywhere. Trade-offs "I pick X because of Y. The cost is Z." "We use Kafka" with no reason. Communication Thinks aloud, checks in, adapts to hints. Silent for 5 minutes, ignores hints. Go deeper Questions to ask in step 1 (copy this list) Users: Who uses it? How many daily active users (DAU)? Features: What are the 3 must-have features? What can we skip? Read vs write: Is it read-heavy (feed, search) or write-heavy (logging, chat)? Latency: How fast must it feel? Real time (chat) or a few seconds is fine (email)? Consistency: Is it OK if a like count is a few seconds late? Is it OK if money is? (No.) Data: How big is one item? How long do we keep it? Region: One country or global? How to draw the high-level diagram (always the same skeleton) Start left to right: Client → DNS / CDN → Load balancer → API servers → Database . Add storage for big files (object storage like S3) if there are images or videos. Add a cache in front of the database for hot reads. Add a queue + workers for slow work (sending emails, processing video, fan-out). Write the 3 to 5 APIs next to it: POST /photos , GET /feed ... Then walk one request through the diagram out loud. That proves it works. How to choose what to deep dive Pick the part that is hard because of scale , not the part that is easy. Ask: "Which component breaks first at 100x traffic?" Typical answers: Feed systems: fan-out on write vs read, celebrity users. Chat: delivering messages in real time, offline users, ordering. Payments: no double charge (idempotency), consistency. Uber: finding nearby drivers fast (geohash), location updates. URL shortener: unique ID generation, redirect latency (cache). The hardest part here is the feed for users who follow celebrities. Let me go deep on that. Common mistakes Jumping into a database choice before knowing the read/write pattern. Over-engineering: microservices, Kafka and Kubernetes for 1,000 users. Saying a tool name without the reason. Always pair a choice with a trade-off. Forgetting failure: what happens when a server, cache or region dies? Running out of time on estimates. Round numbers aggressively (1 day ≈ 100,000 seconds).

sdVisual.title: Building blocks: every box you will ever draw
sdVisual.text: Almost every system is built from the same ~14 Lego bricks. Learn what each brick does , why it exists and what it costs , and you can design anything. Click any box in the big diagram. Follow a READ request (view a photo) Follow a WRITE request (upload a photo) Stop Click a box to learn about it, or follow a request. Cheat sheet: which block solves which problem? Problem you hear Block to add Why "Users are far away, images load slowly" CDN Copies static files to servers near the user. "One server cannot handle the traffic" Load balancer + more app servers Spreads requests over many identical servers. "The database is slow on reads" Cache, read replicas Serve hot data from memory, or from copies. "The database is too big or too busy on writes" Sharding Split data across many databases. "This task takes long (video, email)" Queue + workers Reply to the user now, do the work in the background. "We need to store large files" Object storage Cheap, unlimited, durable file storage. "Search by text or fuzzy match" Search index Inverted index finds words fast. "Many clients, many services, auth everywhere" API gateway One front door for auth, rate limits, routing.

sdVisual.title: Databases: the part interviewers dig into most
sdVisual.text: The database is usually the first thing to break . You need to know how to pick one, how an index makes it fast, what ACID and isolation really mean, and how replicas help reads. 1. SQL or NoSQL? Answer 4 questions There is no "better" one. Pick by the shape of your data and how you query it. Side-by-side comparison SQL (MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle) NoSQL (MongoDB, Cassandra, DynamoDB, Redis) Data shape Tables with fixed columns and relations Documents, key-value, wide rows, graphs Queries Any query with JOINs, flexible Fast for the access patterns you designed for Transactions Strong ACID across rows and tables Usually per item or per partition Scaling Vertical first, then replicas, sharding is manual work Built to scale out horizontally Good for Payments, orders, users, inventory Feeds, chat messages, sessions, logs, catalogs Orders and payments need transactions, so I keep them in PostgreSQL. Chat messages are huge, append-only and read by conversation, so Cassandra keyed by conversation_id fits better. 2. How an index makes a query fast Without an index the database reads every row (full scan). A B-tree index is like a phone book: jump to the right page in a few hops. find id Search with B-tree index Search with full scan B-tree index pages table rows (ids), read one by one in a full scan Pick an id and compare. Watch the "rows touched" count. How it works The B-tree keeps keys sorted in pages. Each page points to child pages for smaller and bigger ranges. To find 61: look at the root, go to the child for 50-74, then the leaf. 3 page reads instead of 27 rows. For 1 billion rows a B-tree is only about 4 levels deep. That is why indexed lookups take milliseconds. Trade-offs and mistakes Writes get slower: every insert must update every index on the table. More storage: each index is a copy of the column plus pointers. Composite index order matters: an index on (city, age) helps WHERE city=? and WHERE city=? AND age=? , not WHERE age=? alone. Functions on columns break indexes: WHERE LOWER(email)=? cannot use a plain index on email. Low-cardinality columns (gender, boolean) rarely benefit. I add an index on (user_id, created_at) because the feed query is "latest posts by user". Writes get a bit slower, which is fine for this read-heavy system. 3. ACID, shown with a bank transfer Transfer 100 from Asha to Ravi. Two steps: take 100 from Asha, give 100 to Ravi. What if the server crashes in between? Transfer normally Crash in the middle (no transaction) Crash in the middle (with transaction) Press a button. A: Atomicity All steps happen, or none. A crash rolls back the half-done transfer. C: Consistency Rules always hold: balance never negative, total money unchanged. I: Isolation Two transfers at the same time do not see each other's half-done work. D: Durability Once committed, it survives a crash (written to the disk log first). 4. Isolation levels: what can go wrong with two transactions Two transactions run at the same time. Weaker isolation is faster but allows strange results called anomalies . Pick an anomaly and play it. Dirty read Non-repeatable read Phantom read Lost update Level Dirty read Non-repeatable Phantom Notes Read Uncommitted possible possible possible Almost never used Read Committed prevented possible possible Default in PostgreSQL, Oracle Repeatable Read prevented prevented possible* Default in MySQL InnoDB (*mostly prevented there) Serializable prevented prevented prevented Safest, slowest, may abort and retry How to fix lost updates in real code Atomic update: UPDATE account SET bal = bal - 100 WHERE id = 1 AND bal >= 100 . The database does read and write in one step. Pessimistic lock: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE locks the row until commit. Simple, but others wait. Optimistic lock: add a version column. UPDATE ... SET version = 6 WHERE id = 1 AND version = 5 . If 0 rows changed, someone else won: reload and retry. In JPA this is @Version . For seat booking I use optimistic locking with a version column. sdVisual.title: Key concepts, explained with pictures
sdVisual.text: These ideas come up in every design round. For each one: the simple picture first, then open the sections for how it works, a real example, trade-offs and the exact words to say. CAP theorem: what happens when the network breaks Data is copied on two servers. If the cable between them breaks (a partition ), you must choose: refuse requests to stay correct ( CP ), or answer with maybe-old data to stay up ( AP ). mode CP: consistency first AP: availability first Break / fix the network Write x = 2 on Node A Read x from Node B Reset Break the network, write on A, then read on B. Try both modes. How it works and PACELC Partitions will happen in any distributed system, so P is not optional. The real choice is C or A during a partition. PACELC adds the normal case: E lse (no partition), choose L atency or C onsistency. Waiting for all replicas to agree is consistent but slower. System During partition Normal times Bank ledger, PostgreSQL primary CP Consistency Cassandra, DynamoDB (default) AP Latency MongoDB (majority writes) CP Consistency Interview answer and mistakes For the wallet balance I choose CP: better to show an error than a wrong balance. For the like counter I choose AP: a slightly old count is fine and the app stays up. Mistake: saying "we pick CA". No partition tolerance means a single machine. Mistake: one choice for the whole system. Different data can make different choices. Consistency models: when will others see my write? After you update something, how soon do readers see it? Play each model. Strong Eventual Read-your-writes Where each is used Strong: every read sees the latest write. Bank balance, inventory count at checkout, seat booking. Eventual: replicas agree "soon" (ms to seconds). Likes, views, follower counts, DNS. Read-your-writes: you always see your own changes, others may lag. Profile edits, your own posts. Monotonic reads: you never see time go backwards (sticky to one replica). Latency vs throughput Latency = how long one request takes (one car's trip time). Throughput = how many requests per second (cars per hour on the highway). More lanes raise throughput but do not make one trip faster. servers (lanes) work per request (ms) Percentiles: why p99 matters more than average p50 = half the requests are faster. p99 = 99 out of 100 are faster. If a page calls 10 services, the chance that at least one hits its slow p99 is about 10%. That is why big companies track p99 and p999. Our target is p99 under 200 ms for the feed API, measured at the load balancer. Scale up vs scale out Vertical = buy a bigger machine. Horizontal = add more machines. Click and compare. Scale UP (bigger server) Scale OUT (add a server) Kill one server Reset Try both, then kill a server. Trade-offs Vertical Horizontal Simplicity No code changes Needs a load balancer and stateless servers Limit Biggest machine you can buy Almost unlimited Failure One box = single point of failure One box dies, others continue Cost Gets very expensive at the top end Cheap commodity machines Start vertical for the database (simpler), scale app servers horizontally from day one because they are stateless. Stateless services: why session data must leave the server If a server keeps your login in its own memory, the load balancer must always send you to that same server. If it dies, you are logged out. Move state to a shared store and any server can answer. State in server memory State in Redis (stateless servers) Send request Kill server 1 Reset Send a few requests, kill server 1, send again. Monolith vs microservices A monolith is one big app deployed together. Microservices split it into small apps that talk over the network. Click "change payments" to see what each one has to redeploy. Monolith Microservices Deploy a change to Payments Payments has a memory leak Reset Pick a style and press a button. Trade-offs and when to choose Monolith Microservices Start speed Fast, simple Slow: infra, CI/CD, discovery Deploy Whole app every time Each service

sdVisual.title: Security: login, tokens and safe connections
sdVisual.text: Authentication = who are you? Authorization = what are you allowed to do? Think of an airport: the passport check proves who you are, the boarding pass decides which plane you can board. AuthN vs AuthZ in one request Real example in Spring Boot Spring Security runs a filter chain. A JWT filter checks the token (authentication) and fills SecurityContext . Then @PreAuthorize checks roles (authorization). 401 means "who are you?", 403 means "I know you, but no". Sessions vs JWT A session is a ticket number; the server keeps the real data in its store. A JWT is a signed ID card; all the data is inside the token, so the server just checks the signature. Session cookie JWT Session JWT Where data lives Server store (Redis) Inside the token Each request Lookup in store Just verify signature (no lookup) Logout / revoke Easy: delete the session Hard: token valid until expiry (use short expiry + refresh token, or a deny list) Best for Classic web apps Mobile apps, microservices, APIs JWT decoder: see what is inside a token A JWT is three Base64 parts joined by dots: header . payload . signature . Anyone can read it. Only the server with the secret can sign it. Edit the payload and watch the signature break. payload (edit me, JSON) {"sub":"omkar","role":"USER","exp":1795000000} Sign with server secret Attacker changes role to ADMIN token Press "Sign". Rules to remember Never put passwords or secrets in the payload. It is only encoded, not encrypted. Always check exp , the signature and the algorithm (reject alg: none ). Keep access tokens short (5 to 15 minutes) and use a refresh token to get new ones. The demo signature here is a simple hash for teaching. Real JWTs use HMAC-SHA256 or RSA. OAuth 2.0: "Login with Google" OAuth lets an app act for you without ever seeing your Google password . Google gives the app a short code, and the app swaps the code for a token on its back end. Step through it. Key words explained Authorization code: one-time code sent through the browser. Useless alone. Client secret: only the app's back end knows it, so only it can swap the code for a token. PKCE: for mobile and single-page apps that cannot keep a secret: the app sends a random hash first and proves it later. Scopes: what the app may do ("read email", not "delete account"). OpenID Connect: OAuth plus an ID token that says who the user is. "Login with Google" is OIDC. HTTPS / TLS handshake, simplified Before any data flows, browser and server agree on a secret key nobody else knows, and the browser checks the server's certificate so it knows it is really talking to the bank. Why it matters in design TLS usually ends at the load balancer or API gateway (TLS termination); inside the network services may use mTLS (both sides show certificates). TLS 1.3 needs only 1 round trip; connection reuse (keep-alive, HTTP/2) avoids repeating the handshake. Certificates expire. Automate renewal (Let's Encrypt, cert-manager). Other must-know basics Password storage Never store plain or MD5. Use bcrypt or Argon2 with a random salt per user. Slow hashing makes brute force expensive. API keys Identify a calling app, not a user. Send in a header, rotate, never commit to git. SQL injection Never build SQL with string concat. Use prepared statements or JPA parameters. XSS Escape user content before showing it in HTML. Angular escapes by default. CSRF A bad site makes your browser send a request with your cookie. Use CSRF tokens or SameSite cookies. Rate limiting Stop brute force and abuse. Open the rate limiter lab

sdVisual.title: Bottleneck finder: classic problems and their fixes

sdVisual.title: Back-of-envelope estimation
sdVisual.text: Estimates tell you which problems are real . 100 requests per second fits one server; 100,000 does not. You do not need exact math, only the right order of magnitude. Round hard and say your assumptions out loud. Numbers to memorize Thing Value Seconds in a day 86,400 ≈ 10^5 Requests per day → per second divide by 10^5 1 million per day ≈ 12 per second 1 billion per day ≈ 12,000 per second Peak traffic 2x to 3x the average One app server ~1,000 to 10,000 simple requests/s One SQL database ~5,000 to 10,000 simple queries/s Redis ~100,000 ops/s per node Powers of two (storage) Power Exact-ish Name 2^10 1 thousand 1 KB 2^20 1 million 1 MB 2^30 1 billion 1 GB 2^40 1 trillion 1 TB 2^50 1 quadrillion 1 PB Typical sizes: a tweet 300 B, a user row 1 KB, a photo 300 KB to 2 MB, 1 minute of HD video ~50 MB. Worked example, step by step Twitter-like Instagram-like WhatsApp-like DAU (millions) writes/user/day reads/user/day item size (KB) Calculate step by step How to present estimates (2 minutes, not 10) State assumptions: "200 M daily users, each posts 2 times and reads 100 times a day." Traffic: writes/s and reads/s (divide by 10^5), then peak = 3x. Storage: writes per day x size x 365 x years. Bandwidth: reads/s x size. Say what it means: "40,000 reads per second at peak, so we need caching and many app servers." Want the full calculator? Open the estimation calculator

sdVisual.title: Scaling and latency
sdVisual.text: A system grows in steps. Add a part only when the current setup starts to hurt. Knowing latency numbers tells you which part to add. Scaling journey Drag the slider. New boxes light up when you need them. users Latency numbers (log scale) Each step down is roughly 10x to 1000x slower. Memory is fast, disk is slow, the network between regions is slowest. show as human time (1 ns = 1 second) Remember Memory read: about 100 ns. SSD read: about 150 microseconds. Same-datacenter network hop: about 0.5 ms. Cross-continent: about 150 ms. So: cache hot data in memory, keep calls inside one region, and avoid chatty service-to-service calls. Reads usually outnumber writes 10 to 100 times, so the first fix is nearly always a cache and read replicas. In an interview say "I would start with one server and one database, then add a load balancer, cache and read replicas as traffic grows. I would shard only at the end, because it is hard to undo." Go deeper How it works, step by step 1 One server: app + DB on one box 2 Split DB onto its own machine 3 Add a load balancer and more app servers 4 Add cache and read replicas 5 Add CDN, queues, then shard the DB 6 Multiple regions Real-world example Most Indian startups follow exactly this path: a single EC2 box with Spring Boot + PostgreSQL, then RDS, then an ALB with autoscaling, then Redis, then read replicas, and only much later sharding. Trade-offs Every step adds moving parts and cost. Do not jump to step 6 for 10,000 users. Caching and replicas fix reads; only sharding fixes write volume. Latency numbers show why: memory is ~100,000x faster than a cross-continent round trip, so keep hot data close and in memory. Common mistakes Designing for 100 M users when asked for a small internal tool. Ignoring the network: a page that makes 30 sequential service calls is slow no matter how fast each one is. Mixing ms and microseconds: a Redis read is ~0.5 ms, a disk seek ~10 ms, India to US ~200 ms.

sdVisual.title: Load balancing and hash ring
sdVisual.text: A load balancer spreads requests over servers. A consistent hash ring decides which server owns a key, and moves very few keys when servers come and go. Load balancer Click a server to take it down or bring it back. Amber dots are slow requests that stay open. algorithm Round robin Least connections Hash of user id Send 10 requests Reset Consistent hash ring 24 keys sit on a circle. Each key belongs to the next node clockwise. Add a node Remove a node virtual nodes (3 per node) Remember Round robin is simplest. Least connections is better when requests take different times. Hashing gives stickiness. Plain hash % N moves almost every key when N changes. A ring moves only about 1/N of them. Virtual nodes spread each server around the ring so load is even. Layer 4 balancers route by IP and port (fast). Layer 7 route by URL or header (smart). In an interview say "I would put a layer 7 load balancer in front of stateless servers with health checks. For a cache or sharded store I would use consistent hashing with virtual nodes." Go deeper How it works, step by step 1 Client hits the LB's single address 2 LB checks which servers are healthy 3 Algorithm picks one: round robin, least connections or hash 4 Request forwarded; response returns through the LB Real-world example Consistent hashing is used by DynamoDB, Cassandra and many cache clusters. Adding a 5th cache node moves only about 1/5 of the keys instead of nearly all of them. Trade-offs Round robin is simple but ignores slow servers; least connections adapts to load. IP or key hashing keeps a user on one server (useful for caches) but can create hot spots. Virtual nodes (each server appears many times on the ring) spread keys evenly. Common mistakes Forgetting the LB itself needs redundancy. Using plain hash(key) % N: changing N remaps almost every key. Sticky sessions instead of stateless servers: a dead server logs users out. Code

sdVisual.title: Caching strategies
sdVisual.text: A cache keeps popular data in fast memory. The two questions: how do writes reach the cache , and what do you throw out when it is full . Write strategies Cache-aside App reads cache first. On a miss it reads the database and fills the cache. Good for Most apps. Simple and safe. Write-through Every write goes to cache and database together. Good for Data that must be fresh. Slower writes. Write-back Write to cache first, flush to database later. Good for Heavy writes. Risk of data loss if cache dies. Write-around Write to database only. Cache fills on the next read. Good for Data written once and rarely read. Eviction: LRU vs LFU (cache size 3) LRU drops the item unused for the longest time. LFU drops the item used the fewest times. accesses Run both Remember Set a TTL on cached items so stale data expires on its own. Cache stampede: many requests miss at once and hit the database. Fix with locking or early refresh. Invalidation is the hard part: delete the key on update rather than trying to patch it. Redis: in-memory, rich types, optional persistence. CDN: caches static files near the user. In an interview say "I would use cache-aside with a TTL and LRU eviction, and delete the key on writes. I would watch the hit rate." Go deeper How it works, step by step 1 Read: check cache first 2 Miss: load from DB 3 Store in cache with TTL 4 On update: write DB, then delete the cache key Real-world example Product pages on Flipkart-style sites are cache-aside in Redis with a TTL; prices are invalidated on change. Sessions and carts often live only in Redis. Trade-offs Cache-aside: simple, cache only holds what is read, but the first read is slow. Write-through: cache always fresh, every write is slower. Write-back: fastest writes, risk of losing data if the cache dies. LRU suits recency (feeds); LFU suits long-term popularity (top products). Common mistakes Updating the cache and the DB in the wrong order, leaving stale data. Prefer: update DB, then delete the key. No TTL: stale data forever and memory fills up. Caching everything: low hit rate, wasted memory. Forgetting cache stampede on hot keys (see Bottleneck finder). Code

sdVisual.title: Replication, sharding, quorum
sdVisual.text: Copy data for safety and read speed (replication). Split data for size and write speed (sharding). Quorum rules decide how sure a read is. Replication and failover Async replication is fast but followers lag. If the leader dies before copying, those writes are lost. Write a value Replicate one step Kill the leader Reset Sharding strategies Three shards. Range is easy to query but can make hot spots. Hash is even. Directory is flexible but needs a lookup service. keys Place keys Quorum: N, R, W If R + W is bigger than N, a read always touches at least one copy with the newest value. N copies 3 5 W (write acks) R (read from) CAP in one table When the network splits CP system AP system Behaviour Refuses some requests to stay correct Answers every request, may be stale Examples HBase, etcd, ZooKeeper, bank ledger Cassandra, DynamoDB (default), DNS Use for Payments, inventory counts Feeds, likes, carts Remember Pick a shard key with many values and even traffic. Bad key (country, date) means a hot shard. Cross-shard joins and transactions are painful, so design queries around the shard key. Replication lag: after a write, read from the leader (or same session) if the user must see it. In an interview say "I would replicate for availability and read scaling, shard by user id with hashing once one database cannot hold the writes, and use quorum reads only where I need strong consistency." Go deeper How it works, step by step 1 Writes go to the leader 2 Leader streams changes to followers 3 Data is split into shards by a key 4 Quorum: write to W nodes, read from R nodes; if R + W > N you read the latest Real-world example Cassandra with N=3, W=QUORUM(2), R=QUORUM(2) gives strong reads per key. A bank's core ledger instead uses one primary with a synchronous standby. Trade-offs Range sharding keeps ranges together (good for scans) but creates hot shards (all new orders on the last shard). Hash sharding spreads load evenly but range queries hit every shard. Directory sharding is flexible but the directory becomes a critical service. Higher W or R = more consistent but slower and less available. Common mistakes Sharding by a low-cardinality key (country): one shard gets India. Cross-shard joins and transactions everywhere: pick a key that keeps related data together (shard orders by customer_id). Forgetting resharding: plan with consistent hashing or many logical shards mapped to fewer machines.

sdVisual.title: Rate limiting
sdVisual.text: A rate limiter says no when a client sends too many requests. Two common ways: token bucket and sliding window. Try both with the same traffic Token bucket: capacity 5, refills 1 token per second. Sliding window: at most 5 requests in any 10 seconds. Send 1 request Burst of 5 Wait 1 second Wait 5 seconds Reset Remember Token bucket allows short bursts, then a steady rate. Good default. Fixed window is simplest but allows a double burst at the window edge. Sliding window avoids this. In a cluster, keep counters in Redis (atomic INCR with expiry, or a Lua script). Return HTTP 429 with a Retry-After header. Limit by user id, API key or IP. In an interview say "I would use a token bucket per user stored in Redis, enforced at the API gateway, returning 429 with Retry-After." Go deeper How it works, step by step 1 Identify the caller (user id, API key, IP) 2 Look up its counter or bucket in Redis 3 Allow if under the limit, else return 429 4 Send headers: limit, remaining, retry-after Real-world example Login endpoints allow ~5 attempts per minute per account; public APIs like GitHub give 5,000 requests per hour per token and return 429 with Retry-After. Trade-offs Token bucket allows short bursts and is easy to explain. Fixed window is simplest but allows 2x bursts at the window edge. Sliding window log is exact but stores every timestamp; sliding window counter approximates it cheaply. Central Redis counter = accurate across servers but adds a network hop; local limits are fast but approximate. Common mistakes Limiting only by IP: many users share an office or mobile carrier IP. Not making the Redis check atomic (use INCR + EXPIRE or a Lua script). Returning 500 instead of 429 so clients retry immediately. Code

sdVisual.title: Queues and Kafka
sdVisual.text: A queue lets one part hand work to another without waiting. Kafka splits a topic into partitions ; each partition is read by one consumer in a group. Partitions and consumer group Same key always lands in the same partition, so order per key is kept. More consumers than partitions means idle consumers. key Produce Produce 6 random Consume one each consumers Reset Remember Order is guaranteed inside a partition only, not across the topic. Delivery: at-most-once (may lose), at-least-once (may repeat, so make consumers idempotent), exactly-once (costly). Use a queue to smooth traffic spikes, run slow jobs (email, video), and decouple services. Dead-letter queue: park messages that keep failing so they do not block others. In an interview say "I would put slow work on Kafka keyed by order id, run a consumer group, and make the consumer idempotent because delivery is at-least-once." Go deeper How it works, step by step 1 Producer sends a message with a key 2 Key decides the partition (same key, same partition, same order) 3 Messages are appended to the partition log and kept for days 4 Each consumer in a group owns some partitions and commits its offset Real-world example An e-commerce OrderPlaced topic with 12 partitions keyed by order_id: payment, email and analytics are separate consumer groups, each reading every message at its own pace. Trade-offs More partitions = more parallel consumers, but ordering is only within a partition. Kafka keeps messages (replay is possible); RabbitMQ deletes after ack but has richer routing. At-least-once delivery is the default: consumers must be idempotent. Common mistakes More consumers than partitions: the extra ones sit idle. Using a random key when order matters (all events of one order must share a key). No dead-letter topic: one bad message blocks the partition forever. Committing the offset before processing: a crash loses the message. Code

sdVisual.title: Resilience and reliability
sdVisual.text: Things fail all the time. Stop calling a dead service , retry politely , make repeats safe , and undo half-finished work. Circuit breaker 3 failures in a row open the circuit. After 5 seconds one trial call decides. downstream service is healthy Call it Wait 5 seconds Reset Retry with backoff and jitter Wait longer each time (1s, 2s, 4s...). Jitter stops all clients retrying at the same moment. add random jitter Show another run Idempotency key A retry after a timeout must not charge twice. Pay 100 (no key), then retry Pay 100 with key, then retry Reset Saga: undo with compensation No big database transaction across services. Each step has an undo step instead. fail at nothing fails Payment Inventory Shipping Run order Remember Always set timeouts on remote calls. No timeout means threads pile up and the caller dies too. Idempotency key: client sends a unique id, server stores the result and returns it on repeats. Saga: choreography (events) or orchestration (a coordinator). Orchestration is easier to follow. Bulkhead: separate thread pools per dependency so one slow service cannot use all threads. In an interview say "Every remote call has a timeout, retries with exponential backoff and jitter, and a circuit breaker. Payment calls carry an idempotency key. Multi-service flows use a saga." Go deeper How it works, step by step 1 Set a timeout on every remote call 2 Retry only safe operations, with backoff and jitter 3 Open the circuit after many failures; fail fast with a fallback 4 Use idempotency keys so retries never double-charge 5 For multi-service workflows, use a saga with compensating steps Real-world example UPI and card payments send an idempotency key (transaction reference) with every request. If the response is lost and the app retries, the bank returns the first result instead of charging twice. Trade-offs Retries improve success but multiply load during outages. Circuit breakers protect the system but users see fallbacks or errors sooner. Sagas avoid distributed locks but the system is briefly inconsistent and you must write undo logic. Common mistakes No timeout: threads pile up waiting forever and the caller dies too. Retrying non-idempotent POSTs without a key. Using two-phase commit across microservices (slow, fragile) instead of a saga. Code

sdVisual.title: What happens when you type a URL
sdVisual.text: This is the classic question. Walk the request from browser to database and back , naming each building block. Step through Previous Next Polling vs long polling vs SSE vs WebSocket Server events happen at seconds 3, 6.5 and 9. How fast does the client learn, and how many requests does it cost? method Polling every 2s Long polling Server-Sent Events WebSocket Remember Polling: simplest, wasteful. SSE: server to client only, auto-reconnects, works over plain HTTP. WebSocket: two-way, good for chat and games. Use WebSocket when the client also sends often. Use SSE for notifications and live feeds. At scale, WebSocket servers hold open connections, so you need sticky routing or a pub/sub layer between servers. In an interview say "For notifications I would use SSE or WebSocket behind the load balancer, with Redis pub/sub to fan messages out between servers." Go deeper How it works, step by step 1 Browser cache, then DNS lookup 2 TCP + TLS handshake 3 HTTP request travels via CDN / load balancer 4 Server runs code, queries cache/DB 5 Response returns; browser parses HTML, loads CSS/JS/images, renders Real-world example Typing your bank's URL: DNS returns the CDN edge, TLS proves the certificate, the WAF and load balancer forward to the web tier, which calls core banking services, then the page renders. Trade-offs Each step can be cached: browser cache, DNS cache, CDN cache, app cache. HTTP/2 and keep-alive reuse connections so the handshake happens once. Common mistakes Forgetting DNS and TLS entirely. Not mentioning caching at each layer. Going too deep into one layer (TCP flags) and never finishing the journey.

sdVisual.title: API design and pagination
sdVisual.text: A good API is predictable : nouns in URLs, verbs in HTTP methods, and safe paging for long lists. Offset vs cursor pagination Newest first, 4 per page. Watch what happens to the repeated item when new data arrives. Next page A new item arrives Reset REST cheat table Action Request Success List orders GET /orders?limit=20&cursor=abc 200 Get one GET /orders/42 200, 404 if missing Create POST /orders (+ Idempotency-Key) 201 + Location Replace PUT /orders/42 200 Change a field PATCH /orders/42 200 Delete DELETE /orders/42 204 Remember Offset is easy but slow on deep pages (database skips rows) and can repeat or skip items. Cursor is fast and stable. Status codes: 400 bad input, 401 not logged in, 403 not allowed, 404 missing, 409 conflict, 429 too many, 5xx server fault. Version the API ( /v1/ ) and never break existing fields. PUT, DELETE and GET are idempotent. POST is not, unless you add a key. In an interview say "I would use cursor pagination for feeds, versioned REST endpoints, and idempotency keys on POST." Go deeper How it works, step by step 1 Name resources as nouns: /users/42/orders 2 Use the right method: GET read, POST create, PUT replace, PATCH update, DELETE 3 Return proper status codes 4 Paginate lists with a cursor 5 Version the API: /v1/ Real-world example Twitter, Slack and Stripe all use cursor pagination: the response carries next_cursor, and the client sends it back to get the next page, so new items do not shift pages. Trade-offs Offset is simple and allows jumping to page 50, but gets slow on big tables and skips or repeats items when data changes. Cursor is fast and stable, but you cannot jump to an arbitrary page. REST is simple and cacheable; gRPC is faster between services; GraphQL lets clients pick fields. Common mistakes Verbs in URLs (/getUser). Returning 200 with an error message inside. Unbounded lists with no pagination. Breaking changes without a new version. Code

sdVisual.title: News feed fan-out
sdVisual.text: When someone posts, do you push it into every follower feed now, or let followers pull it when they open the app? Celebrities break the push model. Compare the costs Assume every user follows 200 accounts. Hybrid pushes for normal users and pulls for celebrities (above 10,000 followers). poster followers Remember Push (fan-out on write): fast reads, expensive writes, wasted work for inactive users. Pull (fan-out on read): cheap writes, slow reads that need many queries. Hybrid: push for most, pull and merge for celebrity posts. This is what big feeds do. Store each feed as a Redis list of post ids. Fetch post bodies in one batch. In an interview say "I would use hybrid fan-out: push into follower feed lists through a queue, but skip celebrities and merge their recent posts at read time." Go deeper How it works, step by step 1 User posts 2 Push model: write the post id into every follower's feed list 3 Pull model: at read time, fetch recent posts of everyone you follow and merge 4 Hybrid: push for normal users, pull for celebrities Real-world example Instagram and Twitter use the hybrid: most posts are pushed into followers' Redis feed lists, while posts from accounts with millions of followers are merged in at read time. Trade-offs Push: very fast reads, heavy writes (a celebrity post = millions of writes), wasted work for inactive followers. Pull: cheap writes, slow reads that query many users. Hybrid: best of both, more complex code. Common mistakes Picking push without mentioning the celebrity problem. Storing full posts in every feed instead of just ids. Forgetting pagination of the feed itself.

sdVisual.title: Geohash, bloom filter, base62
sdVisual.text: Three small tools that appear in many designs: geohash for nearby search, bloom filter for cheap "have I seen this?", base62 for short URLs. Geohash: click the map Each extra character shrinks the box. Nearby places share a prefix, so a prefix search finds neighbours. precision Bloom filter (16 bits, 3 hashes) All 3 bits set means "maybe in set". Any bit empty means "definitely not". It can give false positives, never false negatives. word Add Check Reset Base62 short code 0-9, a-z, A-Z gives 62 symbols. 7 characters give 62^7, about 3.5 trillion short links. id number Encode Remember Geohash edge case: two close points can have different prefixes, so also search the 8 neighbouring boxes. Quadtrees and S2 are alternatives. Use a bloom filter before a slow lookup: crawler seen-URLs, "username taken", cache penetration guard. Short URL: generate a unique id (counter or ID service), encode in base62, store id to long URL. Do not hash and truncate without handling collisions. In an interview say "For nearby drivers I would index locations by geohash in Redis and query the cell plus its 8 neighbours." Go deeper How it works, step by step 1 Geohash: split the map into a grid, each cell gets a string; nearby places share a prefix 2 Bloom filter: k hash functions set k bits; if any bit is 0 the item is definitely absent 3 Base62: turn a numeric id into a short string using 0-9, a-z, A-Z Real-world example Uber/Ola find nearby drivers by geohash prefix (plus neighbouring cells). Browsers and databases use Bloom filters to skip lookups (Cassandra checks a Bloom filter before reading a disk file). URL shorteners turn id 125 into "21" in base62. Trade-offs Geohash cells near boundaries: always search the 8 neighbouring cells too. Bloom filters give false positives (says maybe when it is no) but never false negatives; you cannot delete items from a basic one. Base62 of a counter is short and unique but predictable; add randomness if codes must be hard to guess. Common mistakes Searching only the user's own geohash cell. Using a Bloom filter where a false positive is dangerous without a real check after it. Generating short codes by random strings without checking collisions. Code
